content.title: About
content.content: Beef brain is an organ meat from cattle, with a very soft, creamy, delicate texture and a mild flavor when cooked. It has traditionally been eaten in various cuisines, such as in fried, scrambled, and simmered dishes. Because of safety rules related to prion disease, its sale and use are restricted or banned in many countries.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Beef brain has a very soft, custard-like texture when cooked.
It is part of traditional cuisines in Latin America, the Middle East, South Asia, and parts of Europe.
Brain tissue is very high in fat and cholesterol.
In many countries, cattle brain is classified as specified risk material because of the risk of bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE), and its sale for human consumption is restricted or banned.
It cooks quickly and is usually soaked, cleaned, and blanched before further cooking.

items.title: Source of protein
items.content: Beef brain provides protein.

items.title: Rich in vitamin B12
items.content: Vitamin B12 supports red blood cell formation and nervous system function.

items.title: Provides fats
items.content: Brain contains fats, including some omega-3 fatty acids.

items.title: Provides minerals
items.content: Brain contains phosphorus, copper, and selenium.

items.title: Traditional delicacy
items.content: Beef brain is valued for its texture in several traditional cuisines.

items.title: Prion disease risk
items.content: Cattle brain can carry the prions that cause BSE, which is linked to variant Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease in people. In many countries it is banned or tightly controlled, so only buy it from sources allowed by local regulations.

items.title: Very high in cholesterol
items.content: Brain is among the foods highest in cholesterol, so people with certain health conditions should avoid it or ask a healthcare professional.

items.title: Foodborne illness
items.content: Brain spoils quickly and must be cooked thoroughly to at least about 71 °C (160 °F).

items.title: Purines and fat
items.content: Brain contains purines and a lot of fat, which matters for people with gout.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Beef brain is typically soaked in cold water, the membrane is removed, and it is blanched or simmered before being sliced and pan-fried, scrambled with eggs, breaded, or added to curries. Make sure it is cooked thoroughly. Buy it only from a licensed, regulated source and in places where it is legal.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Beef brain is highly perishable. Keep it refrigerated and cook it within a day, or freeze it for longer storage. Cooked brain should be refrigerated in an airtight container and eaten within a day or two. Discard any brain that smells off.

content.title: About
content.content: Beef liver is an organ meat from cattle that has been eaten in many cultures for centuries. It has a distinctive, rich flavor and a dense, tender texture when cooked properly. Beef liver is considered one of the most nutrient-dense foods and is used in dishes such as pâté, stews, and pan-fried preparations with onions.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Liver is an organ meat, also known as offal, and plays a major role in storing nutrients in the animal.
It is among the most nutrient-dense foods, per serving, in terms of vitamins and minerals.
Liver cooks very quickly and becomes tough and dry if overcooked.
Soaking liver in milk is a traditional way to soften its strong flavor.
Liver-based dishes such as pâté and fried liver with onions are traditional in many cuisines.

items.title: Rich in vitamin A
items.content: Beef liver is a very concentrated source of vitamin A (retinol), which supports vision and the immune system.

items.title: Excellent source of vitamin B12
items.content: Vitamin B12 supports normal red blood cell formation and nervous system function.

items.title: Provides easily absorbed iron
items.content: Liver contains heme iron, which the body absorbs more readily than iron from plants.

items.title: Contains folate and other B vitamins
items.content: These nutrients support normal cell division and energy metabolism.

items.title: High in protein and copper
items.content: Liver provides protein as well as copper, which supports normal iron metabolism.

items.title: Very high vitamin A content
items.content: Regularly eating large portions can lead to excess vitamin A. Pregnant women are commonly advised to limit or avoid liver and should follow their doctor's guidance.

items.title: Cholesterol and purines
items.content: Liver is high in cholesterol and purines, so people with gout or certain heart-related conditions should ask a healthcare professional about it.

items.title: Copper and iron intake
items.content: Frequent consumption can add a lot of copper and iron, which matters for people with related metabolic conditions.

items.title: Foodborne illness
items.content: Undercooked liver can carry bacteria and parasites and should be cooked thoroughly.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Beef liver is usually sliced thin and quickly pan-fried with onions, or braised, grilled, or blended into pâté. Do not overcook it, but make sure it is cooked through. It is eaten in small portions and not every day. Mixing it into ground meat dishes can also soften its flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh raw liver in the refrigerator and cook it within one to two days. For longer storage, freeze it tightly wrapped. Cooked liver should be refrigerated in an airtight container and eaten within three to four days. Thaw frozen liver in the refrigerator.

content.title: About
content.content: Dried blueberries are blueberries (Vaccinium corymbosum) that have been dehydrated to a low moisture level. They retain the characteristic sweet‑tart flavor, bright color, and most of the nutrients found in fresh berries.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Blueberries are considered a “superfood” because of their high antioxidant content, especially anthocyanins.
Dried blueberries store much longer than fresh ones—up to 12 months when kept properly.
In the United States, blueberries are primarily grown in Michigan, Oregon, and Washington, and the dried form is popular as a snack and baking ingredient.
Dried berries are often used in energy bars and granola mixes.
Blueberry is the state fruit of Michigan.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Dried blueberries contain anthocyanins that help combat free radicals and support cellular health.

items.title: Eye health support
items.content: Flavonoids in blueberries may improve night vision and reduce age‑related eye decline.

items.title: Vitamin C source
items.content: Vitamin C boosts immunity and participates in collagen synthesis.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: The natural sugars are concentrated, but dried blueberries still raise blood glucose slowly, which is beneficial for glucose control.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience an allergic reaction to berries of the cranberry family.

items.title: Sugar concentration
items.content: Drying concentrates natural sugars, so people monitoring sugar intake should watch portion size.

items.title: Added ingredients
items.content: Some manufacturers add sugar or preservatives; always check the ingredient list.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Dried blueberries can be eaten as a snack, added to oatmeal, yogurt, baked goods, salads, or used in energy bars. If a softer texture is desired, soak them in water for 10‑15 minutes before use.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. For long‑term storage, keep them in the refrigerator or freezer. Discard any berries that show signs of mold or off‑odors.

content.title: About
content.content: A calzone is a folded pizza made from dough, filled with meat, cheese, and tomato sauce. The crust is usually thin, while the filling stays juicy, making the dish hearty and satisfying.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The name comes from the Italian word “calzone,” meaning “trouser” or “pocket.”
Traditionally calzones are baked in a wood‑fired oven, but they can also be prepared in a regular home oven.
Unlike open‑face pizza, a calzone is sealed, which helps retain more moisture in the filling.
There are countless filling variations, from classic ham and mozzarella to vegetables and seafood.
In the United States, calzones are often served with marinara sauce for dipping.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: The meat provides high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Source of calcium
items.content: Cheese contributes calcium, supporting bone and tooth health.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Meat is a good source of iron, important for oxygen transport in the blood.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Both meat and cheese supply B6, B12, and riboflavin, which aid energy metabolism.

items.title: Energy dense
items.content: The combination of dough, meat, and cheese provides a quick source of energy for active days.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: Calzones are rich in fats and carbs, so portion control is advisable, especially on weight‑loss diets.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: Cheese and meat can increase saturated fat intake, which may be a concern for heart health.

items.title: Sodium
items.content: Processed meats and cheese often contain a lot of salt; people with hypertension should choose lower‑sodium options.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Cheese can trigger allergic reactions in individuals with lactose intolerance or dairy protein allergy.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the calzone hot, sliced in half. It can be eaten with hands or with a knife and fork. It pairs well with marinara sauce, a fresh side salad, or a light vegetable side.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2 days. For longer storage, freeze in a freezer‑safe bag for up to 2 months. Reheat until the internal temperature reaches 75 °C.

content.title: About
content.content: A jelly sandwich on wheat bread consists of two slices of whole‑grain wheat bread spread with sweet fruit jelly (commonly strawberry, cherry or apricot). It is a simple, quick, and popular snack loved by both children and adults.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first recorded mention of jelly sandwiches appears in American cookbooks of the early 19th century.
The classic American "PB&J" (peanut butter and jelly) is often simplified to just jelly for a lighter taste.
Wheat bread gives a denser texture and a subtle sweetness compared with white bread.
Jelly can be made from fresh fruit without added sugar, making the sandwich healthier.
In some countries the jelly sandwich is served with a thin layer of butter to balance the sweetness.

items.title: Source of carbohydrates
items.content: Wheat bread provides a quick source of energy through complex carbohydrates.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals
items.content: Fruit jelly supplies vitamin C and small amounts of B‑vitamins, while whole‑grain bread contributes iron and magnesium.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: Whole‑grain wheat bread is rich in fiber, supporting digestion and satiety.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Unlike sandwiches with butter or cheese, a jelly sandwich contains virtually no fat.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Berry‑based jellies are high in antioxidants that help combat free radicals.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Store‑bought jelly often contains added sugar, which can increase calories and affect blood glucose levels.

items.title: Wheat allergy
items.content: People with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity may react to wheat bread.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: Some fruit jellies are acidic and may irritate a sensitive stomach.

items.title: Preservatives
items.content: Commercial jellies may contain preservatives and artificial flavorings.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the sandwich fresh, optionally toasting the bread for a crunchy crust. A thin layer of butter or nut butter can be added for extra flavor. It works well as a quick breakfast, school snack, or light lunch.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep a prepared sandwich in an airtight container in the refrigerator for no more than 24 hours to prevent the jelly from becoming soggy. Store bread and jelly separately: bread in a dry place, opened jelly in the fridge.

content.title: About
content.content: Sweet green pepper is a fresh, uncooked fruit from the nightshade family. It has a crisp texture, mild sweetness and a bright green color. It is eaten raw in salads, snacks and as a side dish.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Green sweet pepper is an unripe fruit that later turns red, yellow or orange.
One pepper provides more than the daily recommended amount of vitamin C for an adult.
It contains a small amount of capsaicin, giving a gentle bite without the burning sensation of hot peppers.
Ancient cultures grew pepper as an ornamental plant and a symbol of fertility.
The edible part is the fleshy wall; seeds and membranes are usually removed.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C supports the immune system, aids collagen synthesis and improves iron absorption.

items.title: Source of antioxidants
items.content: Carotenoids such as beta‑carotene and lutein protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Low‑calorie food
items.content: Pepper is low in calories but high in water and fiber, helping with weight management.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Fiber promotes intestinal motility and a healthy gut microbiome.

items.title: Contains vitamin B6 and folate
items.content: These vitamins are important for metabolism and neurotransmitter synthesis.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to pepper, such as itching, swelling or hives.

items.title: Food spoilage
items.content: If stored at high temperatures, pepper can develop mold or bacterial contamination.

items.title: Digestive discomfort
items.content: Large amounts of raw pepper may cause gas or discomfort in people with sensitive stomachs.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Slice the pepper into strips, cubes or rings and add it to salads, sandwiches, wraps and fresh snacks. It can also be used as a stuffing for filled dishes or as a crunchy garnish for meat and fish.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store peppers in the refrigerator’s vegetable drawer, placed in a perforated bag. Properly stored they stay fresh for 1‑2 weeks. Remove any damaged fruits to prevent spoilage of the rest.

content.title: About
content.content: Cheese and vegetable pizza is an Italian‑style dish made with a medium‑thick crust, topped with tomato sauce, melted cheese, and a variety of vegetables such as bell peppers, tomatoes, onions, and mushrooms. It is served in restaurants and fast‑food outlets as a quick, satisfying meal.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Traditional pizza dough is made from wheat flour, water, yeast, and salt.
The medium crust (3388) offers a balance between a crunchy edge and a soft interior.
The cheese blend often combines mozzarella and cheddar, giving a creamy taste and good stretch.
Vegetables can be fresh or pre‑roasted, enhancing their aroma and flavor.
Pizza gained worldwide popularity after World War II when American soldiers brought it back from Italy.

items.title: Rich in calcium
items.content: The cheese provides calcium, essential for strong bones and teeth.

items.title: Vitamins and antioxidants
items.content: Vegetables like tomatoes and peppers supply vitamin C and lycopene, a powerful antioxidant.

items.title: Protein source
items.content: Cheese and, to a lesser extent, the dough supply animal and plant protein for tissue repair.

items.title: Sustained energy
items.content: The medium crust delivers complex carbohydrates that keep you full longer.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: Vegetables add fiber, supporting healthy digestion.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Cheese may trigger allergic reactions in people with lactose intolerance or milk protein allergy.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Tomato sauce and cheese often contain added salt, so those monitoring sodium intake should eat it in moderation.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: The crust and cheese make the pizza calorie‑rich; portion control is advisable for weight management.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: Wheat‑based dough contains gluten, which can be problematic for individuals with celiac disease.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy the cheese and vegetable pizza hot, sliced into wedges. Optionally drizzle with fresh basil or olive oil for extra flavor. Restaurants often serve it with chili or garlic sauce on the side.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2–3 days. Reheat in an oven or grill to restore crust crispness.

content.title: About
content.content: Pudding from dry mix (487) is a quick‑ready dessert that prepares in minutes by adding milk or water. It comes in several non‑chocolate flavors such as vanilla, caramel, strawberry and banana. The mix contains starch, sugar, flavorings and stabilizers, delivering a smooth, creamy texture.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Dry mixes allow pudding preparation without eggs.
Vanilla flavor is often enriched with natural extracts rather than artificial aromatics.
Caramel version may contain a small amount of butter for a richer taste.
Strawberry pudding is frequently colored with natural berry juice or powder.
Banana flavor is achieved using dried banana flakes.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: Sugar and starch provide quick glucose, making it a convenient snack.

items.title: Calcium
items.content: Some variants are fortified with calcium, supporting bone health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Vitamins B1, B2 and B6 help carbohydrate metabolism.

items.title: Easy digestion
items.content: Egg‑free and dairy‑free preparation (when using plant milk) suits people with mild lactose intolerance.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: Preparing with a generous amount of liquid contributes to fluid intake.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Dry mixes often contain high sugar levels, which may be unsuitable for diabetics or those watching weight.

items.title: Allergens
items.content: Ingredients may include milk, soy or nuts; check the label if you have allergies.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: A serving can be calorie‑rich due to added sugars and fats.

items.title: Artificial additives
items.content: Some flavors use artificial aromas and colorants that could trigger reactions in sensitive individuals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Pour hot milk, water or a plant‑based drink over the mix, stir thoroughly and let stand 2–3 minutes until thickened. Serve as a standalone dessert, top with fresh berries, nuts, honey or a sprinkle of cinnamon.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the dry mix in a sealed container in a cool, dry place away from direct light. After opening, use within 3–4 months. Discard if it develops off‑odors or changes color.

content.title: About
content.content: Stuffed pepper with meat is a classic dish where a sweet bell pepper is filled with a mixture of ground meat (usually beef or pork), rice, onion, and spices, then baked until tender. The dish combines the juiciness of the meat with the natural sweetness of the pepper.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Stuffed peppers are popular in many cuisines, from Mediterranean to Eastern European kitchens.
Traditional recipes often add tomato paste or sauce to the filling for extra moisture and flavor.
Large peppers are chosen for stuffing because they hold the filling well and stay intact during baking.
The dish is commonly served with mashed potatoes or a fresh salad.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: The meat filling provides high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Bell peppers are an excellent source of vitamin C, which supports immunity and iron absorption.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: Both the pepper and the rice add fiber that aids digestion.

items.title: Provides minerals
items.content: The dish supplies iron, potassium, and magnesium, important for heart and muscle function.

items.title: Moderate carbohydrate content
items.content: Compared with many casseroles, stuffed peppers have a moderate amount of carbs, making them suitable for a balanced diet.

items.title: Sodium overload
items.content: The filling often contains salt; people with hypertension should monitor their intake.

items.title: Meat allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to certain types of meat or spices used.

items.title: Proper cooking
items.content: Meat must be fully cooked to avoid food‑borne illness.

content.title: How to Cook
content.content: Remove seeds from the peppers, prepare a filling of ground meat, rice, onion, spices, and tomato sauce. Stuff the peppers, place them in a baking dish, add a splash of broth or water, cover with foil and bake at 180 °C for 35–45 minutes, then uncover and bake an additional 10 minutes until the tops are golden.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cool the cooked dish to room temperature, then store in an airtight container. Keep in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. Reheat in the oven or microwave until thoroughly heated.
